# ggplot theme setting

```{r}
# plot setting
large <- theme(legend.title = element_text(size=20),
        legend.text = element_text(size=20),
        axis.title = element_text(size=15),
        axis.text = element_text(size=15),
        strip.text = element_text(size=20))
large2 <- theme(legend.title = element_text(size=20),
        legend.text = element_text(size=20),
        axis.title = element_text(size=20),
        axis.text = element_text(size=15),
        strip.text = element_text(size=20))
vert_x <- theme(axis.text.x.bottom = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, face="italic"))
no_strip.x <- theme(strip.background.x = element_blank(),
                  strip.text.x = element_blank())
no_strip.y <- theme(strip.background.y = element_blank(),
                  strip.text.y = element_blank())
no_legend <- theme(legend.position = "none")

# Standard error function
se <- function(x, ...)sd(x, ...)/sqrt(length(x))

load(file="../Rdata/mis.rda") # Marine Isotope Stage
load(file="../Rdata/spp.rda") # Raw species count
load(file="../Rdata/sam.rda") # Sample information
load(file="../Rdata/div.rda") # Diversity

zero <- rowSums(spp)==0 # The sample with zero count

dat <- melt(div, id.vars = c("Age_ka", "Period", "Period2", "SST", "TOC", "TN", "TP", "TIC", "Dino"), measure.vars = c("DAR", "d0", "d1", "d2", "e1","e2")) %>% group_split(variable) 
names(dat) <- c("DAR", "d0", "d1", "d2", "e1","e2")
dat[2:6] <- lapply(dat[2:6], FUN=function(x)x[!zero,])
# log10+1 transformation for Rhizosolenia hebetata; log10 transformation for others
dat <- lapply(dat, FUN=function(x) {x$log10value <- log10(x$value); return(x)})
```

# Standardized Hill numbers at 90% sample coverage 

The standardized Hill numbers were computed in the RMarkdown file **"Okhotsk_Diatom_Alpha_Diversity.Rmd."** In this section, we will load the saved data directly to analyze the diversity indices. The calculation includes species richness (0D), Shannon diversity (1D), and Simpson diversity (2D), all of which were standardized at a sample coverage of 90%. Additionally, we will assess species evenness by computing the normalized slope of the Hill number profile, which corresponds to the values for evenness (1E and 2E).

# Model tuning and optimization

We examined the non-linear relationships between diatom accumulation rate (DAR), species diversity (0D, 1D, and 2D) and species evenness (1E and 2E) in relation glacial cycles and paleo-environmental variables using machine learning techniques, including Random Forest (RF), Generalized Boosted Regression Modeling (GBM), and Bagged Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS). The model parameters were fine-tuned using repeated bootstrap resampling, conducted five times to divide the data into ten parts. Each part was rotated as a test set (i.e., leaving one part out) for cross-validation, while the remaining parts were used as the training set for model development. The performance and accuracy of each model were evaluated by the same 10-fold cross-validation, repeated five times to calculate the average and standard deviation of the cross-validated root mean squared error (RMSE), R-squared (R²), and mean absolute error (MAE). The machine learning models (RF, GBM, and MARS) were constructed, tuned, and evaluated using the R package caret.

# Random Forest

Random Forest (RF) is an ensemble learning algorithm that constructs multiple decision trees through bootstrap resampling and generates an average prediction based on these trees [(Breiman, 2001)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1010933404324). We developed regression RF models using 1,000 trees, and we fine-tuned the number of variables (mtry) randomly selected at each decision split through repeated 10-fold cross-validation. The variable importances in the RF model were estimated by measuring the mean decrease in model accuracy after permuting the values of each independent variable.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
seeds <- vector(mode = "list", length = 51)
for(i in 1:50) seeds[[i]] <- sample.int(1000, 10)

## For the last model:
seeds[[51]] <- sample.int(1000, 1)

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", repeats = 5, seeds = seeds)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
rf <- lapply(dat, FUN = function(x){
  train(log10value~., data = x[,-10:-11], importance=TRUE, ntree = 1000, na.action = na.omit, 
        method = "rf", tuneLength = 10, trControl = ctrl)
})

rf[[1]]$label <- "DAR"
rf[[2]]$label <- "\"\"^0 * italic(D)"
rf[[3]]$label <- "\"\"^1 * italic(D)"
rf[[4]]$label <- "\"\"^2 * italic(D)"
rf[[5]]$label <- "\"\"^1 * italic(E)"
rf[[6]]$label <- "\"\"^2 * italic(E)"

save(rf, file="../Rdata/rf_concentration.rda")
```

```{r}
load("../Rdata/rf_concentration.rda")
ap_rf <- lapply(rf, FUN=function(x)x$results[row.names(x$bestTune),]) %>% ldply(.id="label")

kable(ap_rf, caption = "Accuracy and performance of the best tune RF model by 10-fold cross validation, repeated 5 times") %>% kable_classic
```

## Variable importance

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=10}
rf[[1]]$label <- "(b)~~~~DAR"
rf[[2]]$label <- "(c)~~~~\"\"^0 * italic(D)"
rf[[3]]$label <- "(d)~~~~\"\"^1 * italic(D)"
rf[[4]]$label <- "(e)~~~~\"\"^2 * italic(D)"
rf[[5]]$label <- "(f)~~~~\"\"^1 * italic(E)"
rf[[6]]$label <- "(g)~~~~\"\"^2 * italic(E)"

lapply(rf, FUN = function(x) {
  data = varImp(x, type = 1)$importance
  data$var <- row.names(data)
  data$var <- factor(data$var, levels=data$var[order(data$Overall)])
  ggplot(subset(data, var!="Age_ka"))+
    geom_bar(aes(x=Overall, y=var), stat = "identity")+
    labs(x="IncMSE", y="", title = parse(text=x$label))+theme_bw() %+replace% large
  }) %>% wrap_plots(ncol=2)

lapply(rf, FUN = function(x) {
  data = varImp(x, type = 2)$importance
  data$var <- row.names(data)
  data$var <- factor(data$var, levels=data$var[order(data$Overall)])
  ggplot(subset(data, var!="Age_ka"))+
    geom_bar(aes(x=Overall, y=var), stat = "identity")+
    labs(x="IncNodePurity", y="", title = parse(text=x$label))+theme_bw() %+replace% large
  }) %>% wrap_plots(ncol=2)
```

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=10}
imp <- lapply(rf, FUN = function(x) {
  data = varImp(x, type = 1)$importance 
  data$var <- row.names(data)
  data$var <- factor(data$var, levels=data$var[order(data$Overall)])
  return(data)
  }) %>% ldply %>% pivot_wider(id_cols = ".id", names_from = "var", values_from = "Overall") %>% as.data.frame
rownames(imp) <- imp$.id
imp <- imp[,-1]

pca <- scale(imp) %>% prcomp
out <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
out$label <- c("DAR", "\"\"^0 * italic(D)", "\"\"^1 * italic(D)", "\"\"^2 * italic(D)", "\"\"^1 * italic(E)", "\"\"^2 * italic(E)")
lab <- data.frame(pca$rotation*4)
lab$label <- row.names(lab)
# Variance explained by PC axes
a1 <- round(summary(pca)$importance[2,1]*100, 1)
a2 <- round(summary(pca)$importance[2,2]*100, 1)

ggplot()+
    geom_label_repel(data=out, aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, label=label), parse=TRUE, size=5)+
    geom_segment(data=subset(lab, label!="Age_ka"), aes(x=0, y=0, xend=PC1, yend=PC2), size=1, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2,"cm")), colour=alpha("red", 0.5))+
    geom_label_repel(data=subset(lab, label!="Age_ka"), aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, label=label), colour="red", fill="transparent", size=5, label.padding = unit(0.2, "lines"))+
    labs(x=paste("PCA1 (", a1, " %)", sep=""), y=paste("PCA2 (", a2, " %)", sep=""), title = "(a)")+  
    theme_bw() %+replace% large2
```

```{r}
predictplot <- function(data) {
  ## Descriptive statistics by MIS stages
  # Top x-axis
  ax2 <- subset(mis, Period=="Interglacial")

  # Minimum and maximum ranges of each panel
  data$logvalue <- data$log10value
  p_range <- data[, c("variable", "logvalue", "fit")] %>% melt(id.var="variable", variable.name="range")

  ax3 <- lapply(group_split(p_range, variable), FUN=function(x)cbind(ax2, ymin=min(x$value, na.rm=T), ymax=max(x$value, na.rm=T))) 
  names(ax3) <- c("DAR", "d0", "d1", "d2", "e1", "e2")
  ax3 <- ax3%>% ldply(.id="variable")
  ax3$label <- factor(ax3$variable, labels= labs)

  # Mid-Pleistocene Transition
  mpt <- c(Start=830, End=1230) %>% as.data.frame %>% t
  mpt <- lapply(group_split(p_range, variable), FUN=function(x)cbind(mpt, ymin=min(x$value, na.rm=T), ymax=max(x$value, na.rm=T))) 
  names(mpt) <- c("DAR", "d0", "d1", "d2", "e1", "e2")
  mpt <- mpt %>% ldply(.id="variable")
  mpt$label <- factor(mpt$variable, labels= labs)
  
  ggplot()+
  geom_rect_pattern(data=mpt, aes(xmin=Start, xmax=End, ymin=ymin, ymax=ymax), pattern="stripe", pattern_alpha = 0.1, fill="transparent", pattern_density = 0.3, colour="black", linetype = 4)+
  geom_rect(data=ax3, aes(xmin=Start, xmax=End, ymin=ymin, ymax=ymax), fill="gray", colour="transparent", alpha=0.2)+
  geom_line(data=data, aes(x=Age_ka, y=log10value), alpha=0.5)+
  geom_line(data=data, aes(x=Age_ka, y=fit), colour="blue")+
  labs(x = "Age (ka)", y = expression("Observed vs. predicted DAR &"~alpha-"diversity"))+
  #scale_fill_viridis_d()+
  #scale_colour_viridis_d()+
  scale_x_reverse(expand=expansion(mult = 0.01), breaks=seq(0, 1550, 50), sec.axis = sec_axis(~.*1, breaks = with(ax2, (Start+End)/2), labels = ax2$MIS))+
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.01))+
  facet_wrap(~label, labeller = label_parsed, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y", strip.position="right")+
  theme_bw()%+replace% large %+replace% vert_x
}
```


# Generalized Boosted Regression Modeling (GBM)

Generalized Boosted Regression Modeling (GBM) method constructs a series of regression trees [(Friedman, 2001)](file:///Users/chihlinwei/My Drive/Projects/Okhotsk Diatoms/Ms/(Friedman, 2001)). Each tree is trained to minimize the residuals of the previous tree, and the results are combined to enhance the overall prediction. This approach enables incremental adjustments to the predictions. In our analysis, we fitted GBM models using a Gaussian error distribution. We fine-tuned various model parameters through repeated 10-fold cross-validation. These parameters included the learning rate (shrinkage), the maximum depth of each tree (interaction.depth), the minimum number of observations required in the terminal nodes of the trees (n.minobsinnode), and the total number of trees to fit (n.trees). The variable influence was calculated as the relative contribution of each predictor to the reduction in model deviance across all trees. 

```{r, eval=FALSE}
gb <- lapply(dat, FUN = function(x){
  train(log10value~., data = na.omit(x[,-10:-11]), distribution = "gaussian", verbose = FALSE,
        method = "gbm", tuneLength = 10, trControl = ctrl)
})

gb[[1]]$label <- "DAR"
gb[[2]]$label <- "\"\"^0 * italic(D)"
gb[[3]]$label <- "\"\"^1 * italic(D)"
gb[[4]]$label <- "\"\"^2 * italic(D)"
gb[[5]]$label <- "\"\"^1 * italic(E)"
gb[[6]]$label <- "\"\"^2 * italic(E)"

save(gb, file="../Rdata/gb_concentration.rda")
```

```{r}
load("../Rdata/gb_concentration.rda")
ap_gb <- lapply(gb, FUN=function(x)x$results[row.names(x$bestTune),]) %>% ldply(.id="label")

kable(ap_gb, caption = "Accuracy and performance of the best tune GBM model by 10-fold cross validation, repeated 5 times") %>% kable_classic
```

# Bagged Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines

Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) is a flexible regression technique that captures complex, non-linear relationships by fitting piecewise linear segments (splines) to the data [(Friedman, 1991)](https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176347963). It adaptively determines the locations of knots in the splines. Bagging MARS involves training multiple MARS models using bootstrapped resampling and combining their outputs. Initially, the MARS models may overfit due to the inclusion of numerous basis functions. Then, a backward stepwise elimination procedure is used to prune the models, reducing them to minimize generalized cross-validation (GCV) errors. In this analysis, we fine-tuned the maximum degree of interaction (degree) and the maximum number of terms in the pruned model (nprune) through repeated 10-fold cross-validation. The variable importance was assessed based on the reductions in GCV.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
bm <- lapply(dat, FUN = function(x){
  train(log10value~., data = na.omit(x[,-10:-11]),
        method = "bagEarth", tuneLength = 10, trControl = ctrl)
})

bm[[1]]$label <- "DAR"
bm[[2]]$label <- "\"\"^0 * italic(D)"
bm[[3]]$label <- "\"\"^1 * italic(D)"
bm[[4]]$label <- "\"\"^2 * italic(D)"
bm[[5]]$label <- "\"\"^1 * italic(E)"
bm[[6]]$label <- "\"\"^2 * italic(E)"

save(bm, file="../Rdata/bm_concentration.rda")
```

```{r}
load("../Rdata/bm_concentration.rda")
ap_bm <- lapply(bm, FUN=function(x)x$results[row.names(x$bestTune),]) %>% ldply(.id="label") 

kable(ap_bm, caption = "Accuracy and performance of the best tune SVM model by 10-fold cross validation, repeated 5 times") %>% kable_classic
```

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=10}
ggplot()+
    geom_label_repel(data=out, aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, label=label), parse=TRUE, size=5)+
    geom_segment(data=subset(lab, label!="Age_ka"), aes(x=0, y=0, xend=PC1, yend=PC2), size=1, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2,"cm")), colour=alpha("red", 0.5))+
    geom_label_repel(data=subset(lab, label!="Age_ka"), aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, label=label), colour="red", fill="transparent", size=5, label.padding = unit(0.2, "lines"))+
    labs(x=paste("PCA1 (", a1, " %)", sep=""), y=paste("PCA2 (", a2, " %)", sep=""), title = "IncMSE")+  
    theme_bw() %+replace% large
```

## Partial dependence plot

```{r, fig.width=16, fig.height=16}
pd <- lapply(bm, FUN=function(x){
  vp = varImp(x)$importance  
  all <- row.names(vp)[order(-vp$Overall)]
  grep("Age_Ka|PeriodGlacial|Period2MPT|Period2Post", all)
  pn <- grep("Age_ka|PeriodGlacial|Period2MPT|Period2Post", all, value=TRUE, invert=TRUE)
out <- NULL
for(i in pn){
  out[[i]] <- partial(x, pred.var = i, grid.resolution = 20) %>% melt(measure.vars = i)
}
return(ldply(out, .id="variable"))
}) 

pd[[1]]$label <- "DAR"
pd[[2]]$label <- "\"\"^0 * italic(D)"
pd[[3]]$label <- "\"\"^1 * italic(D)"
pd[[4]]$label <- "\"\"^2 * italic(D)"
pd[[5]]$label <- "\"\"^1 * italic(E)"
pd[[6]]$label <- "\"\"^2 * italic(E)"

lapply(pd, FUN=function(x){
  ggplot(x)+
  geom_line(aes(x=value, y=yhat))+
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales="free", nrow=1)+
  labs(x="Value", y="Partial Dependence", title=parse(text=x$label[1]))+
  theme_bw() %+replace% large
}) %>% wrap_plots(nrow=6, axes = "collect")
```

## Prediction

```{r}
fit <- lapply(bm, FUN=function(x) predict(x)) %>% unlist
out <- cbind(ldply(dat, .id = "variable"), fit) 
out$label <- factor(out$variable, labels=labs)
```

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
ggplot(out)+
  geom_point(aes(x=fit, y=log10value))+
  facet_wrap(~label, scales="free", labeller = label_parsed)+
  labs(x="Prediction", y=expression(log[10](Observation)))+
  theme_bw() %+replace% large
```

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=16}
predictplot(out)
```

# Ensemble average prediction

The R-squared values from the 10-fold cross-validation indicate that the Random Forest (RF) model has the highest accuracy and performance among the three machine learning algorithms. However, we will calculate the ensemble average of the predictions from RF, Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), and Bagged Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS), weighted by their respective R-squared values from the 10-fold cross-validation.

```{r}
# Predictions from RF, GBM, and SVM
x <- cbind(lapply(rf, FUN=function(x)predict(x)) %>% unlist, 
           lapply(gb, FUN=function(x)predict(x)) %>% unlist, 
           lapply(bm, FUN=function(x)predict(x)) %>% unlist
           ) 
colnames(x) <- c("rf", "gb", "bm")

# R squares of RF, GBM, and MARS
w <- cbind(ap_rf$Rsquared, ap_gb$Rsquared, ap_bm$Rsquared) 
colnames(w) <- c("rf", "gb", "bm")
r2 <- w %>% as.data.frame %>% pivot_longer(cols = c("rf", "gb", "bm"))
r2$Method <- factor(r2$name, levels=c("rf", "gb", "bm"), labels=c("RF", "GBRM", "MARS"))

ggplot(data = r2, aes(x = value, colour = Method)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1.5)+
  labs(x=expression("Cross-validated"~R^2), y="Density")+
  theme_bw() %+replace% large

ggplot(data = r2, aes(y = value, x = Method, fill = Method)) +
  geom_violin()+
  labs(y=expression("Cross-validated"~R^2), x="")+
  theme_bw() %+replace% large

w <- w[match(lapply(dat, FUN=function(x)x$variable) %>% unlist, ap_rf$label), ]

av <- NULL
for(i in 1:dim(x)[1]) {
  av <- c(av, weighted.mean(x[i,], w[i,]))
}

out <- cbind(ldply(dat, .id = "variable"), fit=av) 
out$label <- factor(out$variable, labels=labs)
```

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
ggplot(out)+
  geom_point(aes(x=fit, y=log10value))+
  facet_wrap(~label, scales="free", labeller = label_parsed)+
  labs(x="Prediction", y=expression(log[10](Observation)))+
  theme_bw() %+replace% large
```

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=16}
predictplot(out)
```
